summary: German nouns form the plural in five ways: -(e)n (most feminine nouns: Tomate → Tomaten, Zwiebel → Zwiebeln), -e (often masculine: Kohl → Kohle, Lauch → Lauche; sometimes with umlaut), -er (with umlaut where possible), -s (many loanwords: Chili → Chilis) and no ending (nouns in -chen, many in -el/-er/-en: Radieschen → Radieschen). Learn the plural together with the noun. The plural article is always die; in the dative plural the noun adds -n unless it already ends in -n or -s.

askYourself: Which plural did I learn with this noun (die Tomaten, die Kürbisse, die Radieschen)?
Is it feminine? Then -(e)n is very likely.
Does it end in -chen or -lein? Then the plural has no ending.
Is it a loanword ending in a vowel (Chili)? Then often -s.
Is it dative plural? Add -n if the plural does not already end in -n or -s.
Is the noun countable at all (Knoblauch, Mais, Spinat are normally used in the singular)?

traps: Dative plural adds -n: den Kürbissen, den Salaten – but not after -n or -s: den Tomaten, den Chilis.
Same form in singular and plural: das Radieschen – die Radieschen, die Zucchini – die Zucchini, der Brokkoli – die Brokkoli.
Some food nouns are normally uncountable: Knoblauch, Mais (count with eine Knoblauchzehe, ein Maiskolben).
der Kohl has the rare plural Kohle – the same spelling as die Kohle (coal).
Paprika: zwei Paprika (with a number or article), but standing alone often Paprikas.
